passage: On the long drive to Grandma's in Porto Alegre, Gabriel turned the radio down and glanced at his son. "Paulo, I want to tell you something before it happens, so it isn't a surprise." Paulo, ten, looked up from his comic. "In the next few years your voice will crack and then get deeper. You'll grow hair under your arms and in other places. You'll sweat more. Girls in your class will start having periods, bleeding once a month, and that's completely normal too." Paulo giggled. "Tiago says..." "Tiago's big brother tells a lot of stories," Gabriel said, smiling. "You can ask me anything, any time, even the awkward stuff." Paulo was quiet for a while, then asked three questions. Gabriel answered each one plainly.

qa.q: What was Paulo reading when Gabriel turned the radio down?
What do Paulo's giggle and then his three questions suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at first, then curious and safe enough to ask.

qa.q: Why is it wise that Gabriel talks before the changes happen?
qa.a: Plain, unhurried words ahead of time give Paulo confidence and replace stories like those from Tiago's brother with facts.

qa.q: What would change if Paulo had only Tiago's big brother's stories to go on?
qa.a: He would learn from rumour and might feel scared or ashamed when his body began changing.

grounding: Shows a parent explaining voice changes, body hair and periods ahead of time in plain, calm words, instead of leaving a child to rumour.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Varun, eleven, nudged his father and snorted at a poster about growing up. "Papa, look, that's gross." Two boys nearby sniggered too. Jatin didn't shush him or laugh. "It's not gross. It's just what bodies do. Want to know what it means?" Varun shrugged, which meant yes. In a low, ordinary voice Jatin explained: voices breaking, hair growing, girls getting periods every month, and that none of it is a joke to the person going through it. "If you hear something at school that sounds strange or scary, bring it to me first." Varun thought. "Mihir said periods mean you're sick." "They don't. They mean a body is growing up normally." When the nurse called his name, Varun was still asking questions.

qa.q: What did Varun's shrug suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt a bit embarrassed but curious, and wanted to know without saying so.

qa.q: What did Jatin do instead of shushing or laughing, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He explained calmly and plainly and invited Varun to bring rumours to him first, so Varun learns facts rather than fear.

qa.q: How might a girl in Varun's class feel if boys believed what Mihir said?
qa.a: She might feel ashamed or treated as sick, when her body is simply growing up.

grounding: Illustrates a parent answering a child's giggling with plain, unhurried facts about body changes, so the child learns from a trusted adult rather than rumour.
